content.text: On windows/386 a 64-bit return value comes back split across two registers, so I'll handle that case too:

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='internal/platform/platform_windows.go'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('''	ms, _, _ := procGetTickCount64.Call()
	return time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond, nil''','''	lo, hi, _ := procGetTickCount64.Call()
	ms := uint64(lo)
	if unsafe.Sizeof(uintptr(0)) == 4 { // 386: 64-bit result is split across EDX:EAX
		ms |= uint64(hi) << 32
	}
	return time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond, nil''').replace('\t"time"\n','\t"time"\n\t"unsafe"\n')
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
printf '/systool\n/systool.exe\n/dist/\n' > .gitignore
gofmt -l .; for t in linux/amd64 darwin/arm64 windows/amd64 windows/386; do GOOS=${t%/*} GOARCH=${t#*/} go vet ./... && echo "ok $t"; done; cat go.mod; tree -a -I .git . 2>/dev/null || find . -path ./.git -prune -o -type f -print

content.text:
I've set up the Go module in `/work`. It builds and passes `go vet` for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, plus windows/386 and FreeBSD (which hits the fallback). Running it on this Linux machine printed real kernel version and uptime. The Windows and macOS code has only been cross-compiled, not run on those systems.

**The main choice:** the system calls go through `golang.org/x/sys` (v0.48.0), not the standard library's `syscall` package. `syscall` is frozen and gets no new calls; `x/sys/unix` and `x/sys/windows` are the maintained packages for calls the standard library doesn't expose.

**Layout:**
```
go.mod                      module example.com/systool
main.go                     CLI entry point
internal/platform/
  platform.go               shared types, ErrUnsupported, notes on the file layout
  platform_unix.go          //go:build linux || darwin — uname(2), ioctl(TIOCGWINSZ)
  platform_linux.go         sysinfo(2)
  platform_darwin.go        sysctl kern.boottime
  platform_windows.go       RtlGetVersion, GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo, direct kernel32 call
  platform_other.go         //go:build !linux && !darwin && !windows → ErrUnsupported
```

Each OS has its own file, chosen by filename suffix or `//go:build` tags, and they all provide the same functions (`GetInfo`, `TermSize`, `Uptime`). The rest of the CLI can call them without OS checks. The fallback file means the code still compiles on other systems and returns an error there instead of failing to build.

**Two Windows details:**
- `x/sys/windows` has no wrapper for `GetTickCount64`, so `platform_windows.go` loads it from `kernel32.dll` itself. Copy that pattern for any Windows function `x/sys` doesn't cover. It uses `NewLazySystemDLL`, which only looks in System32, so a planted DLL can't be loaded instead.
- On 32-bit Windows a 64-bit return value comes back in two halves, and the code joins them. Without that, uptime would be wrong on 32-bit Windows.

**Things you'll probably want to change:**
- **Module path:** `example.com/systool` is a placeholder. Rename it in `go.mod` and the import in `main.go`.
- **Go version:** `go mod init` wrote `go 1.27.1` into `go.mod`, so anyone building it needs that version or newer. Lower it if you need to support older toolchains.
- **Example calls:** uname, uptime and terminal size are just examples to show the structure. Replace them with the calls your tool actually needs.
- **Plain syscall numbers:** for Linux calls with no wrapper at all, use `unix.Syscall(unix.SYS_..., ...)`.

I also added a `.gitignore` for the built binary. Nothing is committed yet.
